posts.author: andyl
posts.content_md:
So I have taken the DCG plunge, (well at least getting my feet wet).

been getting a little stir-crazy waiting for my next batch of VRP to arrive to do more stereograms, so I am 

begining to experiment with DCG. I have read lot's of papers and posts, and I want to post what I am doing

and planning to try, just to see if I'm on the right path, since there is soo much information scattered everywhere

and every paper does things a little bit different, and there are soo many damn variables. here goes..

Plate preparation

-----------------

I took 6 old 2.5x2.5 plates (pfg03) bleached, scrubbed, and cleaned them nicely.

decided on trying a batch of 8-30-250 dcg. (just figured to start somewhere)

1. I put the 30g of gelatin in 250ml of distilled water (room temp, aprox 22c)

2. waited 30min

3. heated to 60c and stirred for 10min

4. added 8g AmDi and stirred for 10min (under safelight now)

5. filtered solution thru 2 coffee filters into squirt bottle

6. kept warm in waterbath keeping dcg between 50-60c

7. setup plates using "dave blatin" veil coating method

 7a. heated plates with heat gun to about 50-60c

 7b. coated plate with squirtbottle

 7c. waited 5sec

 7d. applied another coat

 7e. moved plate to drying area (empty box from pfg03)

8. wait 24hrs.

------------------------------------------

This is where I am now, I coated the plates last night hoping to shoot and process tonight.

here's what I plan on trying first. And where I'm least sure of what I'm doing.

Exposure

--------

Using C315 - 532nm

I need to keep the exposure time down to a minimun since I don't have a very stable enviroment right now.

I plan on doing an imageplaned copy from a old dichromate pendant hologram as a test. (easy to keep it stable relative to plate)

its only about 1-1/2" in size, I setup a beam spread that gives me aprox 500mJ/cm2 at the plate (lasercheck). is this enough?

Most things I have read list the sensitivity seriously falling off at round 514nm, but never really list what it is at 532. 

I suppose that is also a variable based on AmDi concentration, coating thickness?

Processing

----------

Need to figure out what the simplest process is, less steps the easier to debug, so wondering if this would work?

1. Kodak rapid fix w/hardner - 2min

2. Rinse 1min water

3. Soak in water 3-5min (room temp, 22c)?

4. 100% ISO @ 50c 2-3min w/agitation

5. heat gun dry

So here is where I have some questions...

A. Dose using one ISO bath vs. multiple (25/100 - 50/100 - 100/100) yield a more broadband reconstruction?

 a. Is achieving a broadband reconstruction easier to begin with then a specific bandwidth?

B. Is there a difference in using Thermal Hardening (slavich, pfg-04), vs rapidfix w/hardner?

C. Is there a way to measure the emulsion layer thickness. (without some crazy expensive equipment)

And just a general though, question, pondering...

Eventually I would like to make H2 dcg copies of my stereograms, I really like DCG that has a broadband reconstruction, just

soo damn blinding bright, but depth is proportional to reconstruction bandwidth. But would that be the case in a stereogram

H2? since all the slices lie in the same depth plane. (dist from LCD->PLATE) so would the bandwidth of reconstruction affect

the depth of the precieved stereogram? or could it yield a broadband holo with precieved large depth?

-Andy

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
I was going to wait to reply as I don't want to be considered as a DCG hog here but since you are exposing tonight I thought I might give my two cents.

I am not going to comment on anything you have done except I think you will be ok. Emulsion mixtures look good but 250ml for a few 2.5 x 2.5's? I usually cook 100 ml for 10 - 5x7's.

Lay the plate right on the pendant and do a contact copy to so that you can work on processing variables. Gosh knows there are enough of them. Make sure the you turn the pendant over, pseudo facing the coated plate.

I found with Kodak Rapid fixer mix to a 7:1 dilution. I was working with 4:1 and had not so good results.

Water soak at room temp is fine.

Strait to 100% is fine and should yield a nice broadband holo considering gel hardness (many parameters dictate this). What bloom gel did you start with. If it was Knox I belive it to be about 215 or so. Which if great. When you put is in the alcohol have a white spotlight to view the hologram in the alcohol. Keep the alcohol moving and I rotate the tray as I am never shure which way is the reference angle. You should actually start to see the hologram in the alcohol. As soon as you see it keep it in there for another 10 - 15 seconds then take out and blow dry. For some holograms this has taken seconds up to a couple of minutes. After about 2 minutes just blow dry whether you see the holo or not.

I have not tried thermal hardening. With 24 hour old plates I think the Kodak Rapid Fixer with Hardener will work well.

After the hologram is totally dried through all processes you can measure it with a micrometer pretty acurately. But I would not worry about that with the formula and temperatures of the emulsion you are using and heating the plate you are going to be nicely thin enough.

Hope some of this help and encourages you. 

Feel free to call me tonight anytime in between exposures to go over what you got and what can help. I will send you a Private Message with my home phone. I love talking holography.

John.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Yes, I have seen all kinds of presubbing techniques. But again, I have never had a problem with emulsion lifting off plate.

I soak the plates new or used in the Hydrochloric Acid over night. 

I put on disposable medical rubber gloves, no lube and no powder.

I then take them out and over the Hydrochloric Acid container scrub them with a plastic wool (used for the Teflon coated non stick pans) and put them in a tray with water.

I then rinse and scrub them with the scrubby under running water and put them in a second tray of water. 

I then rinse them again under running water rubbing them all over with my hands with are covered with the gloves and put in a rack standing vertically.

After all are in the rack and before all water drops are evaporated I use one paper towel in my left hand to hold the plate and use another fresh paper towel to wipe each side of the plate. You can hear when they are clean and all the water is gone. I then lay then out on a surface coverd with paper towels. I use Brawney Pick a Size (1/2 sheets).

Then I take some fresh half sheet and cut them in half. When I am ready to coat a plate I take a 1/4 sheet and fold it up. I then grab a plate and hold it ready to be coated. I take the folded sheet at make a single pass down the glass to remove any possible dust specks. I then coat and and use the same folded 1/4 sheet to wipe the bottom edge in my viel coat method.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
That's interesting about the drying/polishing routine. I read somewhere that water vapor in the air quickly "bonds" to glass surfaces, and that it's difficult to remove it. I also read about an old method of subbing glass by polishing with tripoli, which would abrade it slightly, presumably exposing "fresh" glass to be coated with gelatin. Although I don't know for sure, it may be possible that the water bound to the surface of the glass can interfere with adhesion.

It looks like John has a good way of subbing plates, and muriatic acid is readily avilable.

As they say, "Whatever works, works."

When diluting acid make sure to add acid to water and never water to acid! This is very important. HCL is very dangerous and proper handling of it is very important. I am not sure what percentage Muriatic is sold at but the 37% HCL I use at work is very dangerous. Gloves, Face Shield and a acid storage cabinet are good things to have.
